definition: The number of insurance claims per unit of exposure, typically expressed per 1,000 policies. It measures how often claims occur within a cohort, independent of claim severity.

The ratio of total claims paid to total premiums collected for a given cohort or time period. A loss ratio above 1.0 means claims exceed premiums. Used as a primary measure of underwriting profitability.

The estimated total net revenue a customer will generate over their entire relationship with the insurer. Calculated from tenure, premiums paid, claims paid, retention probability, and cross-sell potential. Abbreviated as LTV.

A vehicle classification based on the number of driver-operated pedals. One-pedal vehicles are electric vehicles using regenerative braking. Two-pedal vehicles have automatic transmissions (gas and brake). Three-pedal vehicles have manual transmissions (clutch, brake, gas). Used as a candidate rating factor.

A variable used in insurance pricing models to differentiate risk and set premium levels. Examples include age, zip code, vehicle type, and driving record. Adding a new rating factor requires actuarial justification and regulatory filing.

A braking mechanism in electric vehicles that converts kinetic energy back to battery charge when the driver lifts off the accelerator. In one-pedal driving mode, it can decelerate the vehicle significantly without using the friction brake, which may reduce rear-end collision frequency.
A categorical classification of a policyholder's overall risk level. Common tiers include preferred, standard, and high-risk. Determines the base rate multiplier applied to premium calculation.

The estimated likelihood that a policyholder will renew their policy at the next renewal period. Higher retention correlates with higher lifetime value. Typically expressed as a decimal between 0 and 1.

A telematics-based driving behavior score from the Arity platform. Ranges from 0 to 100, where higher scores indicate safer driving patterns. Incorporates metrics like hard braking frequency, night driving percentage, and trip distance patterns.

The regulatory-approved range within which an insurer can adjust individual rates relative to the filed rate plan without requiring a new filing. Typically expressed as a percentage above and below the base rate. Rate changes within the band can be implemented immediately.

The practice of offering additional insurance products to an existing customer. Common cross-sell products include renters, umbrella, and life insurance. Cross-sell count is a component of lifetime value calculation.
